slides.title: For two centuries, painters had a favourite brown.

slides.body:
For centuries, European apothecaries sold ground-up Egyptian mummies as a remedy called "mummia".

People swallowed it, believing it could heal them.

By 1712, a Paris shop called "À la momie" was selling powdered mummy next to its paints and varnishes.

It made a warm, see-through brown. Painters loved it for glazes and shadows.

slides.kicker: The recipe was what it sounds like.
slides.body: Human and even cat mummies were ground up, mixed and sold as a colour.

By 1849 it was described as "quite in vogue". Eugène Delacroix, Lawrence Alma-Tadema and the Pre-Raphaelites are all thought to have used it.

On the shelf, it looked like any other tube.

Painter Edward Burne-Jones refused to believe it, until Alma-Tadema said he had seen a mummy in a paint-maker's workshop.

Burne-Jones took his tube to the garden and gave it a proper burial. His nephew, Rudyard Kipling, helped.

slides.kicker: In the end, the mummies ran out.
slides.body:
The paint also cracked and faded, and artists turned to other browns.

In 1964, a London colour-maker told Time it might have "a few odd limbs" left, but not enough to make any more paint.

slides.lead: Most of what we use every day comes with a story we never ask about.
slides.accent: Ask anyway. The answer might change what you're willing to use.

slides.line: Save this, and ask one more question today.

caption:
For about two centuries, one of painters' favourite browns was made from ground-up Egyptian mummies. When Edward Burne-Jones found out, he buried his tube in the garden. 🎨

What's something you use every day without knowing where it comes from?
